newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian-U.S. crew do repairs on Mir then rest.
newsitem.headline: Russian-U.S. crew do repairs on Mir then rest.

text.p: The Russian-American crew carried out repairs on Sunday to make the stricken space station Mir more stable and were then given the rest of the day off.

Officials at Mission Control near Moscow told Interfax news agency the three-man crew had fixed another of the gyrodine devices which keep Mir's solar panels lined up on the Sun and are vital for steady orientation.
Efforts to repair one more gyrodine had failed but eight of the station's 12 gyrodines were now working, they said.

Despite this success, Russian space officials were expected to announce on Monday that more important and risky repairs to fix the power supply, damaged in a collision on June 25, will be carried out by a crew due to arrive on Mir on August 7.

"I think it is better for us not to propose to this crew that they go out into open space as there is only a little time until the next expedition and the lads are tired," mission director Vladimir Solovyov said on Saturday.
"They have been through a lot, something which has a serious effect on a person's pyschology," he said in a television interview.
Interfax said the crew had a video link-up with MIssion Control on Sunday morning and added: "Mission Control declared July 20 a rest day on the station "
Crew commander Vasily Tsibliyev, flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin and NASA physicist Michael Foale have been dogged by a jinx-like series of problems.

About half of Mir's power was lost during the collision during a manual docking manoeuvre on June 25 which punctured a module attached to the 11-year-old space station. Mir has been limping through space ever since.

Repairing the power supply will require entering the airless module and working in spacesuits for several hours. If the operation goes wrong, Russian space officials say the crew doing the repairs may have to abandon ship.

Problems have continued since the collision. An unidentified liquid leaked into space, tests showed Tsibliyev had an irregular heartbeat and one of the crew caused a computer to crash last Thursday by pulling out a wrong cable.
The computer crash, which plunged the sprawling craft into darkness and left it spinning in space, was fixed on Friday.
Crew commander Tsibliyev, 43, was due on Sunday to have more medical tests, Itar-Tass news agency said.
U.S. officials at Mission Control said Foale hoped to use Sunday to continue experiments which have been interrupted on the impact of space flight on the internal clock of beetles.
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin, 39, are scheduled to return to Earth on August 26, with Foale, who is 40, returning aboard a U.S. shuttle in September.
Russian cosmonauts Pavel Vinogradov and Anatoly Solovyov are in training outside Moscow at Zvyozdny Gorodok to undertake the repair work and are due to blast off for Mir on August 5.

The problems on Mir, which was originally expected to have a usueful lifespan of about five years, have raised doubts about its future and that of Russian cooperation in space with the United States and other nations.
Asked if the United States would end its participation in the Mir project, U.S. President Bill Clinton said last Thursday that it was too soon for him to draw a conclusion.
